cite_as: Naftzger, N., Sniegowski, S., Devaney, E., Liu, F., Hutson, M., & Adams, N. (2015). Washington 21st Century Community Learning Centers Program Evaluation: 2012-13 and 2013-14. AIR for OSPI.
claimed_component: Design: propensity score stratification, 30+ and 60+ day participants vs nonparticipants. Outcome: confirm the size and significance of state math test impacts (expected small or mixed).

cite_as: American Institutes for Research (2013). Rhode Island 21st Century Community Learning Center Evaluation 2011-12: Impact Report.
claimed_component: Design: propensity score stratification, 30+ and 60+ day participants vs same-school nonparticipants. Outcome: math impact not significant; reading about 0.055 SD at 30+ days.

cite_as: White, L., & Whisman, A. (2014). 21st Century Community Learning Centers 2014: A Quasi-Experimental Investigation of Program Impacts on Student Achievement in Mathematics and Reading/Language Arts. West Virginia Department of Education (ERIC ED569910); also White & Hixson (2014), 2013 cohort.
claimed_component: Design: propensity score matched comparison, 30+ day participants. Outcome: no significant differences in year-to-year WESTEST 2 math or reading gains between CCLC and non-CCLC students.

cite_as: Holstead, J., & King, M. H. (2011). High-Quality 21st Century Community Learning Centers: Academic Achievement among Frequent Participants and Non-Participants. Journal of Education for Students Placed at Risk, 16(4), 255-274.
claimed_component: Design: matched comparison, 60+ day attendees at high-quality Indiana centers vs matched nonattendees. Outcome: effects only in math, and only for attendees who failed the fall test.

cite_as: Jenner, E., & Jenner, L. W. (2007). Results from a First-Year Evaluation of Academic Impacts of an After-School Program for At-Risk Students. Journal of Education for Students Placed at Risk, 12(2), 213-237.
claimed_component: Design: quasi-experimental, Louisiana 21st CCLC, outcome ITBS pre and post. Outcome: positive impact for participants attending 30+ days, rising with attendance. Confirm effect size in math and how the comparison group was formed.

cite_as: Zief, S. G., Lauver, S., & Maynard, R. A. (2006). Impacts of after-school programs on student outcomes. Campbell Systematic Reviews, 2006:3.
claimed_component: Design: systematic review restricted to experimental evaluations of after-school programs. Outcome: confirm small or null effects on academic achievement (test scores).

cite_as: Pennsylvania Department of Education (2025). 21st Century Community Learning Centers Program: 2023-24 State Evaluation Report (revised May 6, 2025).
claimed_component: Design: descriptive pre-post by program-hour band with no comparison group. Outcome: share of students improving in math rose from about 14% (<15 hours) to 17% (270+ hours); attendance improvement reported only for students at or below 90% prior attendance.

cite_as: Evans, V., & Wolford, T. (2014). Out-of-School Time Participation and Student Outcomes: An Evaluation Brief. Social Innovations Journal (School District of Philadelphia).
claimed_component: Design: correlational, City of Philadelphia OST records matched to district records. Confirm whether prior achievement or attendance was controlled and the direction for math test scores.

cite_as: Gao, J., Hallar, B., & Hartmann, T. A. (2014). A Snapshot of OST Programs in Philadelphia: An Evaluation of Eleven 21st Century Community Learning Center Grantees. Research for Action (ERIC ED553131).
claimed_component: Design: correlational dosage analysis of participation and outcomes, Philadelphia 21st CCLC grantees. Confirm whether PSSA math was analyzed, the direction, and whether prior scores were controlled.

cite_as: Vandell, D. L., Reisner, E. R., & Pierce, K. M. (2007). Outcomes Linked to High-Quality Afterschool Programs: Longitudinal Findings from the Study of Promising Afterschool Programs (ERIC ED499113).
claimed_component: Design: two-year longitudinal study, about 3,000 low-income elementary and middle school students, eight states. Outcome: regular participation in high-quality programs linked to gains in standardized math test scores; confirm adjustment for prior achievement and the math effect size.

cite_as: Leos-Urbel, J. (2015). What Works after School? The Relationship between After-School Program Quality, Program Attendance, and Academic Outcomes. Youth & Society, 47(5), 684-706.
claimed_component: Design: longitudinal multilevel models, 29 NYC programs, 5,108 students in grades 4-8. Outcome: greater purposeful engagement associated with lower test scores; supportive environment and structured interactions associated with higher scores.

cite_as: Lester, A. M., Chow, J. C., & Melton, T. N. (2020). Quality is Critical for Meaningful Synthesis of Afterschool Program Effects: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Journal of Youth and Adolescence, 49, 369-382.
claimed_component: Design: meta-analysis comparing all studies with high-quality studies only. Outcome: confirm the pooled academic effect among high-quality studies and that including lower-quality studies changed conclusions.

cite_as: Craig, S. D., Hu, X., Graesser, A. C., Bargagliotti, A. E., Sterbinsky, A., Cheney, K. R., & Okwumabua, T. (2013). The impact of a technology-based mathematics after-school program using ALEKS on student's knowledge and behaviors. Computers & Education, 68, 495-504.
claimed_component: Design: randomized trial (WWC: meets standards with reservations), after-school math with ALEKS software and teacher support. Outcome: Tennessee state math test (TCAP) g = 0.07, not significant.

cite_as: Rickles, J. H., & Barnhart, M. K. (2007). The impact of supplemental educational services participation on student achievement: 2005-06. Los Angeles Unified School District.
claimed_component: Design: quasi-experimental (WWC: meets standards with reservations). Outcome: no significant effect of NCLB Supplemental Educational Services tutoring on California Standards Test math or English.

cite_as: Munoz, M. A., Chang, F., & Ross, S. M. (2011). No Child Left Behind and Tutoring in Reading and Mathematics: Impact of Supplemental Educational Services on Large Scale Assessment (ERIC ED528807).
claimed_component: Design: matched treatment-control (SES tutees vs eligible nonparticipating schoolmates), large urban district, fifth year of SES. Outcome: consistently positive but small, nonsignificant effects on state reading and math tests.

cite_as: Rothman, T., & Henderson, M. (2011). Do School-Based Tutoring Programs Significantly Improve Student Performance on Standardized Tests? RMLE Online, 34(6), 1-10.
claimed_component: Design: quasi-experimental (WWC: meets standards with reservations), after-school tutoring for grade 8. Outcome: no significant effect on the New Jersey GEPA mathematics or language arts score.

cite_as: Garcia, I., Grossman, J. B., Herrera, C., Strassberger, M., Dixon, M., & Linden, L. (2020). Aiming Higher: Assessing Higher Achievement's Out-of-School Expansion Efforts. MDRC (ERIC ED606086).
claimed_component: Design: RCT of Higher Achievement in expansion sites (WWC: meets standards without reservations). Outcome: no significant effect on the state math assessment or reading achievement.

cite_as: McKinney, D., Walters, K., Powell, K., et al. (2026). The Impact of NBA Math Hoops on Students' Math Achievement: A Randomized Controlled Trial. WestEd (ERIC ED681343).
claimed_component: Design: RCT; NBA Math Hoops classrooms vs STEM enrichment classrooms, often out-of-school-time settings. Outcome: +0.19 SD on math achievement; three hours of training, free materials, under $20 per student. Confirm the grades, the test (standardized or researcher-made) and the setting (school day or after school).

cite_as: Mac Iver, M. A., & Mac Iver, D. J. (2019). 'STEMming' the Swell of Absenteeism in the Middle Years: Impacts of an Urban District Summer Robotics Program. Urban Education, 54(1), 65-88.
claimed_component: Design: quasi-experimental (WWC: meets standards with reservations), Baltimore summer robotics. Outcome: Maryland School Assessment math effect not significant.

cite_as: Snyder, C., & Stevenson, O. (2021). G2ROW STEM: Girls and Guys Realizing Opportunities with STEM. i3 development grant evaluation (ERIC ED613865).
claimed_component: Design: matched-sample QED within the same schools, Tennessee middle schools, three years of extended-learning STEM. Outcome: TNReady Math g = 0.40 and Science g = 0.32, significant (WWC: meets standards with reservations).

cite_as: CrimeSolutions (National Institute of Justice). Program profile: Citizen Schools Expanded Learning Time (evaluations by Arcaira et al. 2010 and Fountain et al. 2016).
claimed_component: Confirm the CrimeSolutions rating (expected: no effects or ineffective) and which outcomes it rests on, in particular state math test scores.

cite_as: Gordanier, J., Ozturk, O., Williams, B., & Zhan, C. (2020). Free Lunch for All! The Effect of the Community Eligibility Provision on Academic Outcomes. Economics of Education Review, 77, 101999.
claimed_component: Design: difference-in-differences of CEP adoption, South Carolina. Outcome: about 0.06 SD increase in elementary math scores, smaller in reading; confirm middle school results.

cite_as: Dalane, K. (2025). The Impact of Community Eligibility Provision on Multilingual Learner Outcomes. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness.
claimed_component: Design: student fixed effects with CEP rollout. Outcome: math +0.032 SD and reading +0.082 SD for multilingual learners.

cite_as: Corcoran, S. P., Elbel, B., & Schwartz, A. E. (2016). The Effect of Breakfast in the Classroom on Obesity and Academic Performance: Evidence from New York City. Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, 35(3).
claimed_component: Design: difference-in-differences, NYC schools adopting breakfast in the classroom. Outcome: no evidence of gains in academic performance (state test scores).

cite_as: Cuadros-Menaca, A., Thomsen, M. R., & Nayga, R. M. Jr. (2022). Evaluation of Delivering Breakfast after the Bell and Academic Performance among Third-Grade Children: An Application of the Synthetic Control Method. Journal of School Health.
claimed_component: Design: synthetic control, Arkansas schools. Outcome: little evidence of program effects on grade 3 math or reading; any negative math effects were transitory.

cite_as: Frisvold, D. E. (2015). Nutrition and Cognitive Achievement: An Evaluation of the School Breakfast Program. Journal of Public Economics, 124, 91-104 (IRP DP 1402-12).
claimed_component: Design: regression discontinuity on state mandates requiring breakfast where free-lunch share exceeds a threshold. Outcome: availability raises math and reading achievement; confirm the size for math.

cite_as: Bernstein, L. S., McLaughlin, J. E., Crepinsek, M. K., & Daft, L. M. (2004). Evaluation of the School Breakfast Program Pilot Project: Final Report. USDA FNS (ERIC ED486532).
claimed_component: Design: schools randomized to universal free breakfast. Confirm the effect on standardized achievement test scores (expected no significant effect).

cite_as: Gassman-Pines, A., & Bellows, L. (2018). Food Instability and Academic Achievement: A Quasi-Experiment Using SNAP Benefit Timing. American Educational Research Journal, 55(5), 897-927.
claimed_component: Design: quasi-experiment using variation in SNAP benefit issuance timing, North Carolina grades 3-8. Outcome: end-of-grade test scores (math and reading) are lower when tests fall later in the benefit month; confirm direction and size.

cite_as: Duncan, G. J., Morris, P. A., & Rodrigues, C. (2011). Does Money Really Matter? Estimating Impacts of Family Income on Young Children's Achievement with Data from Random-Assignment Experiments. Developmental Psychology, 47(5), 1263-1279.
claimed_component: Design: instrumental variables using random assignment in welfare and antipoverty experiments. Outcome: a $1,000 increase in annual income raises young children's achievement by about 5-6% of a standard deviation; confirm ages at outcome.
